content.title: Before the squash
content.text: The recipe of a neuron: multiply every input by its weight, add the products, add the bias, squash. Take one neuron of the first row of the digit network as it reads the 7, and stop just before the squash. That total is called z. Here z = 0.235. Every one of the 64 pixels had a say in it, through its own wire.
content.ledger:
THE LINE SO FAR
neuron 10, first row · z = 0.235 before the squash

content.title: One pixel moves
content.text: Freeze everything except one pixel, a bright one near the top. The network reads brightness 0 to 16 as a number x from 0 to 1, so slide x from 0 to 1 and watch z. Lay x left to right, z up and down, keep the record, and the record is a straight line. No bend anywhere: each extra bit of x adds exactly the same amount to z.

labels: z = the total before the squash

content.title: A straight line: y = m·x + b
content.text: Every straight line is two numbers. m is the slope: how much y rises for one extra unit of x. Here m = 0.485, and it is the weight on this pixel’s wire, nothing else. b is the lift: where the line sits when x is 0. Here b = −0.068, the other 63 pixels times their weights plus the bias, all frozen into one number. Two numbers, and the whole line is known.

content.title: A weight is a slope
content.text: Pick another pixel and the line changes its tilt. This one, lower down, carries weight −0.507: its line runs downhill, more brightness there pulls z down. This one carries 0.044: nearly flat, the neuron barely listens to it. That is what a weight is. Large means the pixel matters, negative means it pushes the other way, near zero means ignored. This neuron holds 64 slopes, one per pixel.

content.title: The bias is the lift
content.text: The bias is added to the total whatever the pixels say. Turn it and the whole line moves up or down without tilting. It sets how much input the neuron needs before z turns positive: a low bias makes a reluctant neuron, a high one an eager one. Here it is −0.089, a small nudge, but it is the 65th number this neuron owns, and training moves it like any weight.

content.title: Turn the weight instead
content.text: The previous pill turned a weight, so turn this one. Freeze the pixel at its real value, 0.625, and turn the weight from −1 to 1. z moves on a straight line again, and now the slope is 0.625: the pixel. Weight times pixel is the same as pixel times weight, so each is the slope of the other. Keep this: the slope of z against a weight is the input on that wire. It comes back twice later in the series.

content.title: Why a line is not enough
content.text: Lines are simple, and that is the problem. A line goes up forever or down forever; it cannot say ‘this pixel helps up to a point, then hurts’. And a line fed into a line is still a line. Take the squash out of every neuron and the whole network, three rows and 2,778 numbers, collapses into one straight line per score: here, the score for 7 against the same pixel. 650 numbers would do that job. The squash is what prevents the collapse, and its shapes are next.
